Cross-modal transfer, where information from one speech form helps decode another, is a promising remedy; yet how a decoder internally represents and processes brain activity from different speech forms remains unclear. In this work, we ask: which internal neurons of a decoder carry cross-modal information, and are these neurons shared across different speech forms? To answer these questions, we leverage mechanistic interpretability, using recordings of the same sentences in vocalized, mimed, and imagined input pairs for activation patching. We insert the decoder’s internal activity for a sentence in one condition into its processing of the same sentence in another and measure the change in decoding accuracy. We find that no single neuron drives this benefit; instead, it arises from small groups of neurons, with vocalized speech as the most useful source. These groups are largely condition-specific in the early stage of the decoder but overlap in the later stage. candidates.snippet: paper_id=isca-colin01-mmnmcgurk | title=The mismatch negativity (MMN) and the McGurk effect | authors=C. Colin, M. Radeau, P. Deltenre | venue=Proc. candidates.title: Linking speech perception and neurophysiology: speech decoding guided by cascaded oscillators locked to the input rhythm
candidates.snippet: paper_id=pmc-3127251-tempo | title=Linking speech perception and neurophysiology: speech decoding guided by cascaded oscillators locked to the input rhythm | venue=Front. Psychol. | review_state=source_checked | Study.research_objective=Acoustic-feature models of speech perception are incomplete without decoding time. Propose that nested cortical oscillations govern template-matching at hierarchical temporal scales, and build Tempo to emulate the counterintuitive intelligibility profile of time-compressed speech re-packaged by silent gaps | Study.unit_of_analysis=A computational model evaluated against the Ghitza & Greenberg (2009) corpus: sentences compressed into 40-ms packets at varying information-per-packet and packaging rate; predicted error curves (TSM/TFM) compared to human word-error rates | task_encoding=natural_utterance | task_family=sentence_recognition | tested_population=healthy_volunteers | Cohort.demographics=No new participants — simulations benchmarked to published psychophysics (Ghitza & Greenberg 2009 time-compression listeners); clinical extrapolations (aging, dyslexia, cochlear implants) are proposals, not tests | intended_use_cases=research_of_inner_speech, other | demonstrated_use_cases=research_of_inner_speech | production_labels=ordinary_voiced_speech | modalities=scalp_eeg, meg, ecog, fmri, other | Acquisition.sensor_geometry=Model ties observed EEG/MEG/ECoG oscillatory modulations (delta <3 Hz, theta 4–8, beta 15–30, gamma >50) to speech units: phonetic features↔beta, syllables/words (~250 ms)↔theta, prosodic phrases (500–2000 ms)↔delta | representation_kind=Three nested clocks: theta (4–8 Hz, 100–250 ms cycle) parses syllables; ~4 beta cycles per theta handle ~50 ms dyads (diphone-scale segments centered on acoustic edges, captured by coincidence over tonotopic channels); gamma samples rapid spectro-temporal transitions inside dyads; delta aligns to prosodic phrases | ProcessingStep.architecture=Two-path architecture: lower path tracks input rhythm via a PLL (theta = master VCO entraining the cascade), upper path does memory access — TFM computes firing coincidence across frequency channels into dyad neurons each beta cycle, TSM maps dyad-neuron sequences onto a syllable neuron at each theta-cycle end; ASI quantifies uncompressed speech per window | EvaluationProtocol.experimental_design=Emulate compressed speech: information stream chopped into 40-ms packets + silent gaps; ASI = uncompressed ms per window; vary information-per-packet vs packaging rate; TSM/TFM error counts vs theta-cycle fit predict the mirrored-L error profile | EvaluationRun.execution_artifacts=Tempo reproduces the key paradox: word error >50% when packaging rate exceeds theta range, then intelligibility is substantially restored when silent gaps re-align packets to theta cycles — because decoding time, not information density, is the binding constraint | extra.Output.output_kind=A mechanistic bridge between cortical rhythms and speech decoding: oscillators supply the parse-and-match timing — when they can lock, comprehension holds; when packaging outruns theta, comprehension collapses until silence restores sync | Claim.claim_scope=Speech intelligibility is governed by decoding time: cascaded theta/beta/gamma oscillations must remain phase-locked to the input rhythm for template-matching to succeed — hence compression defeats listeners at >50% WER, and silent gaps restore comprehension by restoring lock, a counterintuitive result classical acoustic models cannot explain | Claim.claim_scope=Neurally, a theta master oscillator (VCO-like PLL element) entrains beta and gamma: beta parses ~50 ms dyads across tonotopic channels, theta closes a syllable-neuron match every ~200 ms — implementing multi-scale parsing without a fixed sampling window | extra.Limitation.status=acknowledged | extra.Limitation.limitation=PLL tracking module is explicitly unimplemented — inaccurate rhythm tracking desyncs theta; model validated against one psychophysical corpus; no neural recording data of its own; dyad edge placement is ambiguous for some diphones; aging/dyslexia/cochlear-implant accounts remain hypotheses | 4 cycles | 50 ms | 50% | 200 ms | 250 ms
